We introduce B IG F INANCE B ENCH, a 928-item expert-authored benchmark of open-ended financial-research tasks in which each item pairs a ground-truth reference answer with a point-weighted rubric that decomposes the derivation into independently checkable steps.
the best system reaches only 58.8% rubric score, final-answer accuracy is a useful but lossy proxy for derivation quality, and model capability varies non-uniformly across financial workflows
Existing finance benchmarks largely evaluate isolated subskills or final answers, leaving the auditable derivation itself under-measured.

The dataset contains 928 items authored by 52 financial-research subject-matter experts, predominantly current and former investment bankers and private equity investors, with smaller representation from equity research and adjacent buy-side roles.
A separate panel of 12 reviewers audited the items before inclusion.
The dataset was assembled between September 2025 and March 2026.
Each criterion carries an integer weight on a 1 to 10 scale, with the final answer always carrying a meaningful share of total points.
In the preserved review logs, 81% of items (748 of 928) contain substantive feedback or reviewer-applied edits
By rubric points, the stage mix is 29.5% Retrieval, 5.8% Definition, 63.2% Calculation, and 1.5% Other.
We evaluate current frontier and open-weight models in a common open-book ReAct-style harness with a 50-step budget.
web_search supports broad discovery, edgar_search targets SEC filings, fetch_url retrieves the selected source, and python_exec provides a sandbox for calculation and tabular manipulation
two independent judges (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and Claude Opus 4.7) receive the question, visible agent trace, reference answer, and full point-weighted rubric
The primary metric is rubric score: earned rubric points divided by total rubric points, macro-averaged across questions.
Each model is run for three trials per question.
Inter-judge agreement is high (Cohen’s κ ∈ [0.952, 0.973] on final-answer correctness across the ten models)
Every model sits above the equality line, with a mean rubric-minus-final-answer gap of 15.95 pp
Pro is 8.7 pp above Flash on final-answer accuracy, but Flash is 2.3 pp above Pro on rubric score
no model earns the highest rubric on more than 37.7% of questions under fractional tie credit
the best systems remain below 60% rubric score and below 45% final-answer accuracy
a simple router using observable (workflow, source) features improves over the best single model by 7.6% relative rubric gain and 10.7% relative answer-accuracy gain

A 928-question evaluation of how frontier AI agents perform on the work finance professionals actually do.
FinanceBench grades short-answer extraction against fixed passages. FinQA, FinanceMath, and DocFinQA grade arithmetic against single contexts.
BFB is not a harder version of those benchmarks. It's a different category: workflow-grounded, agent-executed, derivation-graded.

Vertical-specific skills (374): The judgment that distinguishes desks from one another: capital structure and returns, M&A and special situations, valuation, private capital, governance, and capital markets.
Metrics (301): Identifying, collecting, and computing the KPIs that drive a thesis.
Earnings and financial-statement analysis (137): Reading filings the way a financial professional reads them, and understanding what story the numbers tell.
Scenarios and model forecasting (116): Building base, bull, and bear cases from disclosed guidance and management commentary.
The 52 practitioners who wrote the questions also wrote the rubrics, and a panel of 12 senior reviewers stress-tested every one.
Every question carries one, averaging 17 line items, each tagged as Retrieval, Definition, or Calculation, and weighted 1 to 10.
Across the benchmark: 15,656 rubric criteria, 36,241 weighted points.
All questions are designed to have an objective answer, be time-constrained so the answer remains fixed over time
We graded ten frontier systems against BFB - six closed and four open-weight, including the strongest models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Z.AI, Alibaba, Moonshot, and Google DeepMind.
Each model ran each question three times in a minimal agent setup with access to SEC EDGAR, the public web, and a Python sandbox.

We deliberately exclude: vector-store retrieval, premium financial data sources
(FactSet, CapIQ, Bloomberg, etc.), broker research, and provider-specific affordances
edgar_search | SEC EDGAR public REST API

the same surface so the evaluation measures the model, not the scaffold.

**Trials**: each (question, model) pair runs 3 times.
**Judges**: default two-judge panel (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview + Claude Opus 4.7);

**`python_exec` is not a sandbox.** It's a subprocess with a 5-second timeout
  and no filesystem, network, or syscall isolation.

This release contains a 50-question stratified subset of the 928-item BigFinanceBench benchmark, with full reference answers, point-weighted rubrics, traces, and grades.
The remaining benchmark items are held back to mitigate benchmark contamination and preserve evaluation validity.
human_workpapers/: two illustrative calculation workbooks from independent human validation.
Each public trajectory is graded by Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, and GPT-5.5.
The release includes 3 runs per question for each evaluated model.
Evaluated models: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, Gemma 4 31B, GLM-5.1, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen3.6 27B.
Judge models: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and Claude Opus 4.7.
The public subset contains 50 questions, 793 rubric lines, and 1,931 rubric points. Rubrics average 15.86 lines and 38.62 points per question.
Rubric score is computed by summing earned points and dividing by total possible points for the question.
The released subset is stratified by workflow and difficulty quartile and preserves full-benchmark model rankings under rubric score (Kendall's tau = 0.956).
This page tracks frontier model performance on BigFinanceBench: a leaderboard, cost-versus-accuracy view, and a worked example showing how models are graded step by step.
Scores are a two-judge mean (Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7) averaged across model families to limit self-preference.
